title: The Great Stink

lines.text: In the summer of eighteen fifty-eight, London smelled so bad that the government nearly ran away from its own capital.

scene.title: The *Great* Stink
scene.sub: How a summer of horror built the modern city

lines.text: Politicians hung curtains soaked in chloride of lime over the windows of Parliament, just so they could keep working.

scene.headline: Parliament, *soaked* in lime
scene.sub: Curtains drenched in chloride of lime to block the smell

lines.text: The cause was simple, and disgusting.
More than two million people were flushing their waste straight into the river that many of them drank from.
This is the story of how a smell changed the way cities work.
London was growing faster than anyone had planned for.
Homes had cesspits, and the cesspits overflowed into drains that were built for rainwater.
Those drains emptied into the Thames, which was also a source of the city's drinking water.
Doctors had a theory for the disease that followed: bad air, which they called miasma.

scene.headline: Disease travels on *foul air*
scene.sub: That was the belief. It was wrong.

lines.text: In eighteen fifty-four, a physician named John Snow mapped a cholera outbreak in Soho and pointed at a single water pump.

scene.headline: John *Snow* maps the cholera deaths
scene.sub: In Soho they clustered around a single water pump.

lines.text: Most officials weren't convinced. They still blamed the air.
Then came the hot summer of eighteen fifty-eight, and the river began to cook.

events.label: John Snow traces a Soho outbreak to one pump
Work begins on the new sewers

lines.text: Parliament acted within weeks.
The job fell to Joseph Bazalgette, chief engineer of the Metropolitan Board of Works.

scene.headline: Joseph *Bazalgette*
scene.sub: Chief engineer, Metropolitan Board of Works

lines.text: His plan was beautifully simple: stop the waste reaching the river at all.

scene.text: Stop the *waste* reaching the river *at all.*

lines.text: Great sewers would run beside the river, catch everything before it arrived, and carry it east.
Pumping stations lifted it along, and it was released far downstream, on the outgoing tide.
The numbers were enormous: about eighty-two miles of main sewers,

scene.label: of main *intercepting* sewers
scene.sub: plus roughly eleven hundred miles of street sewers

lines.text: roughly eleven hundred miles of street sewers, and more than three hundred million bricks.
And here is the strange part.
Most of the people demanding those sewers believed in miasma, the wrong theory.

right.title: The result
points: Waste kept away from the water

lines.text: But by carrying waste away from the river, they ended up tackling the real cause.
London's last major cholera outbreak came in eighteen sixty-six.
Bazalgette's sewers didn't just clean the river.
Building them also created new land along the Thames, where the Victoria Embankment now stands.

scene.headline: New land beside the *Thames*
scene.sub: The Victoria Embankment was built along the river with a sewer inside it.

lines.text: The pumping stations were built with ornate ironwork, as if the sewers deserved a cathedral.

scene.headline: Sewers with a *cathedral's* ironwork
scene.sub: Pumping stations decorated like grand public buildings.

lines.text: And more than a hundred and fifty years later, much of his network is still in use.

scene.label: later, much of the network is *still in use*

lines.text: A city overwhelmed by its own waste had learned to carry it away.

scene.text: A city *overwhelmed* by its own waste learned to *carry it away.*

lines.text: Thanks for watching.

scene.title: Thanks for *watching*
scene.sub: More stories of how the modern world got built
